meta.title: Claude Haiku 5.5 · Machine learning · solo · 6 hours
meta.note: 6-hour run. The verifier accepted 3 of 4 credited claims; 2 set a new best held-out result on their dataset. Verdicts from the re-run of the official verifier.

artifacts.title: ResNet-9-style CNN with label smoothing, crop/flip augmentation and flip TTA beats the 6% CIFAR-10 reference
artifacts.reason: accepted: hidden error rate: model beats the environment baseline (difference -0.0122, 95% CI [-0.0162, -0.0078], beyond the minimum effect 0.0012)

claim.statement: A ResNet-9-style CNN trained for 100 epochs with one-cycle SGD, label smoothing 0.1, random crop and flip augmentation, and flip test-time augmentation reaches 4.96% error on a 5,000-image held-out split of the CIFAR-10 training set when trained on the other 45,000; the submitted model uses the same recipe trained on all 50,000 images and should beat the 6% reference on the official test set.

artifacts.title: Word+char TF-IDF linear ensemble beats a TF-IDF+logistic-regression replica on AG News
artifacts.reason: accepted: hidden error rate: arm a beats the other arm (difference -0.0176, 95% CI [-0.0220, -0.0134], beyond the minimum effect 0.0020)

claim.statement: On a 5,000-article held-out split of the AG News training set (model fit on the other 35,000), a score-level ensemble of word+char TF-IDF logistic regression, a 1-2gram NB-SVM and word logistic regression reaches 8.84% error versus 10.56% for a TF-IDF (1-2gram) plus default logistic-regression replica; the test trains both arms on all 40,000 articles and predicts the hidden test set, and arm A should have lower error than arm B.

artifacts.title: A 3-seed ensemble of the ResNet-9-style CIFAR-10 recipe beats the 6% reference with margin
artifacts.reason: rejected: claimed numbers do not reproduce within 10% on rerun

claim.statement: Averaging the softmax outputs (with flip TTA) of three ResNet-9-style CNNs, each trained for 100 epochs with one-cycle SGD, label smoothing 0.1, crop and flip augmentation on 45,000 CIFAR-10 training images, gives 4.48% error on the remaining 5,000 training images, against 4.62%, 4.90% and 5.02% for the individual seeds; the submitted ensemble applies the same recipe to all 50,000 images and should beat the 6% reference on the official test set.

artifacts.title: Word+char TF-IDF linear ensemble predicts AG News below the TF-IDF+logistic-regression comparator
artifacts.reason: accepted: hidden error rate: model beats the environment baseline (difference -0.0058, 95% CI [-0.0088, -0.0026], beyond the minimum effect 0.0017)

claim.statement: A score-level ensemble of word+char TF-IDF logistic regression, a 1-2gram NB-SVM and word logistic regression, trained on all 40,000 AG News training articles, has lower error on the official hidden test set than the TF-IDF (1-2gram) plus logistic-regression comparator, which the baselines quote at about 8%; on a 5,000-article split of the training data the ensemble scored 8.84% against 10.56% for a replica of the comparator, so the split is harder than the official test and the margin is measured relative to that replica.

events.text: I'll start by reading the lab guide and available commands before choosing a research direction.
Let me look at the data, baselines, and budget before choosing a direction.

Two datasets, two comparators. CIFAR-10 needs under 6% error, which a well-tuned ResNet trained for a long schedule might reach on this GPU. AG News needs to beat TF-IDF + LR at about 8% error. Before choosing, I'll read the starter script, check for local pretrained weights (no internet), and see which packages are installed.

CIFAR-10 has the clearer path. The reference is 6% error, and a ResNet-9-style network with label smoothing, crop and flip augmentation, a one-cycle schedule and flip TTA should get well under that. I'll write one script with a validation mode (train on 45k, report error on the held-out 5k) and a final mode (train on 50k, save weights, predict the hidden test set). A separate predict-only path will load saved weights for the evaluator. I'll start with a 40-epoch validation run.

The 40-epoch run gives 5.34% validation error on the 5k held-out split, under the 6% reference. Next I'll check whether longer training helps. I'll run 100 epochs with the same recipe.

```bash
cd /work/cifar
EPOCHS=100 lab exec /work/cifar -- python run.py 2>&1 | tail -5
```

The 100-epoch run isn't what I intended. Its log shows epochs 0 to 39 and `val_error` 0.0542, so the `EPOCHS=100` environment variable didn't reach the run. `lab exec` doesn't pass my shell environment through. I'll change the script's default instead, then rerun.

```bash
cd /work/cifar
sed -i 's/get("EPOCHS", 40)/get("EPOCHS", 100)/' run.py
grep -n 'EPOCHS = ' run.py
lab exec /work/cifar -- python run.py 2>&1 | grep -E '"val_error|"epochs|exit_code|val_error' | head -10
```

The 100-epoch run gives 4.96% held-out error, down from 5.34% at 40 epochs. Next I need a final model trained on all 50k images that the evaluator can load. Since `lab exec` doesn't pass my environment variables, I'll switch the mode with a `final.txt` file in the code directory. I'll also record the exec ids.


```bash
cd /work/cifar
python - <<'EOF'
s = open("run.py").read()
s = s.replace('''elif E:
    t = np.load(f"{E}/cifar10/inputs.npz")
    net, mean, std = train(x_all, y_all)''', '''elif os.path.exists("final.txt"):
    # Final evidence run: train on all 50k, save weights for the predi

The final run finished and saved `model.pt`. Next I need the exec ids and the weights' blob id for the contribution, so I'll list the runs and inspect the final exec.

```bash
cd /work/cifar
lab runs
lab show exec-05ccc616 | grep -v '"stdout"' | head -60
```

The final model is trained on all 50k images, so it has no held-out score of its own. The 4.96% number comes from the 45k-trained run, `exec-011a8d98`. Before I publish, I'll check the prediction-only path locally with a fake eval folder built from training images, and read the contribution schema.

```bash
cd /work/cifar
lab schema | head -80
mkdir -p /tmp/fake_eval/cifar10 /tmp/fake_out /tmp/fake_in
python - <<'EOF'
import numpy as np, shutil
d = np.load("/lab/data/cifar10/train.npz")
np.savez("/tmp/fake_eval/cifar10/inputs.npz", x=d["x"][:500], id=np.arange(500))
EOF
shutil.copy if False el

The `lab schema` output confirms the fields I need. Next I'll test the prediction-only path locally. I'll fetch the saved weights, point a fake eval folder at 500 training images, and check the output format and accuracy. This is only a format check, since those images are in the training set.

```bash
cd /work/cifar
ls /tmp/fake_eval/cifar10/
lab fetch 7a40b010a9c9b178893a9e1eb4539cb908fcce269fb6ecb46d30d5046d1cde59 /tmp/fake_in/model.pt
mkdir -p /tmp/fake_out
DATA_DIR=/lab/data EVAL_DIR=/tmp/fake_eval IN_DIR=/tmp/fake_in OUT_DIR=/tmp/fake_out python run.py
head -3 /tmp/fake_out/predictions.c

The prediction-only path works: it loads the saved weights, applies flip TTA, and writes one row per id. I'll publish the CIFAR-10 finding now. The held-out number is 4.96% from `exec-011a8d98`, and the test will run the 50k-trained weights from `exec-05ccc616` on the hidden 10k images.

```bash
cd /work/cifar
lab schema | tail -60
cat > f_cifar.json <<'EOF'
{"kind": "finding",
 "title": "ResNet-9-style CNN with label smoothing, crop/flip augmentation and flip TTA beats the 6% CIFAR-10 reference",
 "claim": {"statement": "A ResNet-9-style CNN trained for 100 epochs with one-cycle SGD, label sm

The `test.inputs` field needs a dictionary, not a list. I'll read the `Test` definition in the schema to get the expected keys.

```bash
cd /work/cifar
lab schema | python -c "import json,sys; s=json.load(sys.stdin); print(json.dumps(s['\$defs']['Test'], indent=1)); print(json.dumps(s['\$defs'].get('Rel'), indent=1))"
```

The `inputs` field takes a name-to-blob mapping. I'll name the weights `model.pt` so they land at `$IN_DIR/model.pt`, which is the path `run.py` globs for. Otherwise the test would silently retrain from scratch.

```bash
cd /work/cifar
cat > f_cifar.json <<'EOF'
{"kind": "finding",
 "title": "ResNet-9-style CNN with label smoothing, crop/flip augmentation and flip TTA beats the 6% CIFAR-10 reference",
 "claim": {"statement": "A ResNet-9-style CNN trained for 100 epochs with one-cycle SGD, label smoothing 0.1, random crop and flip augmentation, and flip test-time augmentation reaches 4.96% erro

A pretrained language model would make a large gain easy, but the earlier search for weight files returned nothing. I'll check again more thoroughly, look at the AG News file format, and see which NLP packages are installed.

Word 1-2gram TF-IDF with LR is the comparator. Adding character n-grams and a linear SVM is cheap and usually gains a point on news topic data. I'll keep the same save/predict structure as the CIFAR script and record every configuration's validation error.
Parse C from the last underscore-separated field, then rerun the same validation sweep.

Validation gives 9.44% error for the best config, `wc_lr_20`. That is worse than the roughly 8% comparator, so this model would not beat the baseline on the hidden test. I'll sweep a wider set of linear models, including lower C values, a Complement Naive Bayes model and an ensemble of their scores, all on the same 5k validation split.

```bash
cd /work/agnews
cat > sweep.py <<'EOF'
import os, json
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from scipy.sparse import hstack
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.naive_ba

If the comparator scores about 9% on my split, the 8% figure is a split effect and my models are on par. If it scores 8%, my split is harder and I need a real gain. NB-SVM is a one-vs-rest model with per-class feature scaling, so I'll implement it directly.
I need to know whether the comparator replica finished before the timeout. Then I'll rerun only the comparator and a 1-2gram NB-SVM with liblinear, in the background, and poll it.
Give the background job a few minutes, then read its progress log and the recorded exec status.
`lab exec` may only write its output when it finishes, so an empty log doesn't mean the job is stuck. I'll check the process list and the recorded runs before deciding whether to wait or restart.
Kill the runaway process, replace `np.diag` with `scipy.sparse.diags`, and rerun the comparator plus NB-SVM in the background.
Find the runaway process by PID, kill it, fix the dense `np.diag` in `sweep3.py`, and relaunch in the background.
Kill only the process whose full command line is exactly `python sweep3.py`, then check that it's gone, apply the sparse-diagonal fix, and relaunch.
Wait for the background job, then read the log and confirm the exec's status. If it's still running with no progress, I'll investigate before relaunching.
Run a small score-level ensemble of wc_lr_3, NB-SVM (1-2gram, C=1) and word LR on the same 5k validation split. Pick weights on validation only, and record every combination so the choice is visible.

Write `run_test.py` to fit the chosen ensemble (LR C=3 on word+char, NB-SVM 1-2gram, word LR C=3 at weight 0.5) and the replica on all 40k articles, then write `predictions_a.csv` (ensemble) and `predictions_b.csv` (replica). Test it on 300 training rows as fake inputs, then store the directory as a blob and get the exec ids for the evidence.
Contribute a `comparison` finding with `better: "a"` (the ensemble). The quantities are the two validation errors, each present in its evidence exec's metrics.json.
Check for messages or other researchers' artifacts that could change what's worth doing, and confirm my two contributions are listed.

Both findings are registered, but the CIFAR margin rests on one seed. A 3-seed ensemble may add accuracy, and I need validation evidence for it before I publish. I'll write `run2.py` with separate modes for validation, ensemble scoring, 50k training and prediction. The seed comes in as an argument because `lab exec` doesn't pass environment variables. Then I'll launch three 45k validation seeds in the background, one exec each, to stay under the 900s block limit.
Sleep for about seven minutes, then check the logs and the recorded runs. The ensemble step needs the saved validation probabilities from each seed, so I need the exec ids and blob ids first.

Seeds 1 and 2 haven't appeared in the run list yet. I'll check whether the background loop is still going, read their logs, and look up how `lab exec` takes `--input` so the ensemble step can read the saved probabilities.
Wait for seed 2, then read the recorded `run2.py val` execs and their `valprobs.npy` blob ids from `lab runs`. The ensemble step needs those ids as `--input` arguments.

The `ens_val` mode averages the three saved probability arrays and scores the average. I'll pass the three blobs as inputs. In parallel I'll start the three 50k-trained models sequentially. Each takes about 6 minutes, and the ensemble check doesn't use the GPU.
Each final model takes about 6 minutes, so all three should finish in about 18 minutes. I'll wait in two sleeps, then read the final execs and their weight blobs from `lab runs`.
Two final models remain. Once all three are recorded, I'll list their `m*.pt` blob ids so the test can load them as `IN_DIR` inputs.

`predict` mode globs `IN_DIR/*.pt` and averages softmax outputs from every file. I'll fetch the three weights, run the mode on the 500 fake eval images, and check the output shape. I'll also read the code blob id from the recorded exec.

Each quantity must appear in an evidence exec's metrics. `ens_val_error` 0.0448 is in `exec-6b51d01b`, and the member errors are in their `run2.py val` execs. The test inputs are named `m0.pt`, `m1.pt`, `m2.pt`, which is the glob `predict` mode reads.

The AG News comparison test only checks the ensemble against my replica, which scored 10.56% on my split but about 8% is quoted for the official comparator. A `prediction` claim against the official 8% baseline would test something more useful. I'll write a prediction-only script for the same ensemble, dry-run it on fake inputs, and store it as a blob.

The quantities are the ensemble's 8.84% and the replica's 10.56%, both in `exec-02d6b30a` and `exec-fabcd4ee`. I'll use the new `run_pred.py` blob as the test code and state the split-difference caveat in the claim.
Use `RandomState(1)` for a fresh 5k validation split, and score the fixed ensemble (weights 1, 1, 0.5) against the replica. If the gap holds, the claim is less likely to be a selection artifact.

The fresh split confirms the linear ensemble's gain over the replica: 8.08% against 9.10%. The gain is about one point, and the official comparator is only quoted at about 8%, so the margin is thin. A different model family could add more. I'll try a from-scratch word-level CNN, which is cheap on the GPU, and test whether adding it to the linear ensemble helps on two independent splits (seeds 0 and 1). The ensemble weight will be chosen on seed 0 and checked on seed 1.
Check that all four findings are still live and list their evidence, then decide whether more work is worth the remaining time.

Four findings are registered and live. The AG News ensemble margin is about 1.5 to 1.7 points over my replica on two splits, and the NN ensemble result was mixed, so I won't add it. A null result would need a preregistration filed before its evidence runs, which I didn't do, so I'll leave it out. The remaining budget won't buy a clearly better model, so I'll close my part of the session.
